References / Poster / 353

The Move and Pink Floyd at UFO

Hapshash and the Coloured Coat’s screen print for the UFO club, London, 1967: a winged woman falling through gold sunburst rays, with lettering that melts from magenta to yellow.

Source
Victoria and Albert Museum: E.1708-1991
Creator
Hapshash and the Coloured Coat (Michael English and Nigel Waymouth)
Made
1967 (The Move on 26 May, Pink Floyd on 2 June)
Style
Psychedelic art (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Hallucinatory, radiant, fluid
Evidence
Downloaded the V&A image of object E.1708-1991 (IIIF, 1067 × 1600 px) to a scratch folder and inspected it. The V&A image shows the sheet rotated 180°; the observations below use reading orientation, with the imprint at top left. The image is not stored.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The V&A catalogues it as a silkscreen poster by Michael English and Nigel Waymouth (Hapshash and the Coloured Coat) for The Move and Pink Floyd at UFO, Great Britain, 1967. It describes “pink through orange to yellow rainbow lettering with gold on white ground” and an upside-down woman with butterfly wings. The inscription at top left reads “1007 © UFO 1967”. V&A.

Hapshash’s silkscreen posters advertised London happenings, clubs, and concerts and helped start the sale of posters as art. The V&A owns many originals and held the retrospective “Cosmic Visions: Psychedelic Posters from the 1960s” in 2000–2001. Wikipedia.

Observed

  • Broad rays of metallic gold radiate from the center of the sheet across white paper.
  • A woman in white silhouette falls head-down through the middle. Her butterfly wings and robe are filled with scale, bubble, and droplet patterns cut out of the gold.
  • Two blocks of swollen, rounded lettering sit lower left and lower right. Each blends from magenta at the top through orange to yellow at the bottom.
  • Sprays of fine gold dots soften the edges of the rays near the figure.
  • There is no rectangle or frame. The rays run off every edge.

Why it belongs

The magenta-to-yellow lettering is the split-fountain rainbow effect that the rubric names, done in screen print. It carries all the color on a sheet that is otherwise gold and white.

The sunburst is the radiating-ripple motif in its simplest form, a useful background for a hero area.

Borrow

Run one warm two-color blend through the display lettering and keep everything else flat.

Use a full-bleed sunburst of broad rays as the ground behind a central figure.

Fill a silhouette with a repeating scale or bubble pattern instead of shading.
